A night with ayahuasca in the Peruvian Amazon

The ceremony began at dusk in a round wooden maloca, the smoke of mapacho tobacco drifting between the rafters while the shaman, an old man with a quiet voice, blew it over each of us before handing out the first small cup of the brew.

I had read that the medicine tastes of earth and rot, and it did. Within an hour the darkness of the room was no longer empty: thin lines of light began to draw geometric patterns behind my closed eyelids, repeating and folding into one another like a tunnel that kept opening in front of me, each ring a copy of the last one at a smaller scale.

The icaros, the chanting of the shaman, seemed to push the tunnel forward. When the nausea came I vomited into the bucket beside my mat, as everyone around me did, and I was told this is part of the purge. Afterwards the visions grew calmer and I felt presences that I could almost name, as if the plant were introducing its teachers one by one.

In the morning, over a plate of rice and plantains, the other participants described almost the same corridor of shifting geometry, the same sense of being watched by something ancient and patient. A retired anthropologist among us said that sceptics usually arrive convinced it is a chemical trick, and leave unable to explain why it felt like a place rather than a dream.

The active compounds are DMT and harmala alkaloids; the smoke, the songs and the darkness are what turn a pharmacological event into a ritual that people remember for decades.
